# Findings: WAF Analysis of DDoS Flood against cf-httpecho.a.example.com

**Source:** CloudWatch Logs Insights on log group `aws-waf-logs-group` (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1). WebACL `shield-sample-webacl`. All queries filtered to `httpRequest.host = "cf-httpecho.a.example.com"`. All timestamps UTC, 2026-09-08.

## 1. Flood shape & timeline (per-minute req count)
| Minute (UTC) | Requests | Phase |
|---|---|---|
| 03:45–04:14 | ~31–32/min | Baseline (steady) |
| **04:15** | 2,332 | **Onset** |
| 04:16 | 104,192 | Ramp |
| 04:17 | 120,032 | **Peak (rate-capped plateau)** |
| 04:18 | 120,031 | Peak |
| 04:19 | 120,031 | Peak |
| 04:20 | 117,512 | Peak |
| 04:21 | 16,092 | Tail / decline |
| **04:22** onward | ~31–32/min | **Recovered to baseline** |

- **Onset:** 04:15 UTC. **Peak:** ~120,031 req/min sustained 04:17–04:19 (the flat ~120K plateau indicates a per-rule evaluation cap). **Subsided:** by 04:22. Flood active window ≈ 7 minutes (04:15–04:21).

## 2. Request disposition over time
- Baseline and non-flood minutes: ~31–32 **ALLOW**/min, 0 BLOCK.
- 04:16 (WAF catching up): **72,530 BLOCK + 31,662 ALLOW** — brief leak window where flood requests slipped through before the rate counter tripped.
- 04:17–04:20: **~120,000 BLOCK/min**, ALLOW back down to baseline ~31–32/min — WAF fully clamped the flood.
- 04:21: 16,060 BLOCK (tail), then 0.
- **No CHALLENGE, CAPTCHA, or COUNT actions occurred** — the flood was handled purely by BLOCK.

## 3. Terminating rule (what stopped the flood)
| terminatingRuleId | terminatingRuleType | action | Requests |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`rate-limit`** | **RATE_BASED** | BLOCK | **566,070** |
| `Default_Action` | REGULAR | ALLOW | 36,790 |

- The dominant mitigation was the rate-based rule **`rate-limit`**, which BLOCKed **566,070** flood requests. The 36,790 ALLOW consists of baseline legit traffic (~32/min across 90 min ≈ 2,900) plus the ~31,662 flood requests that leaked during the 04:16 ramp before the rate threshold tripped.

## 4. Anti-DDoS detection evidence (exact label strings)
Only two distinct `awswaf:` labels appear in the window:

| Exact label string | Count | First seen | Last seen |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`** | **566,070** | **04:16:13.599** | 04:21:19.109 |
| `awswaf:managed:token:absent` | 36,790 | 03:45:01.196 | 05:14:59.018 |

- The Anti-DDoS managed rule group label **`awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`** was stamped on exactly the 566,070 BLOCKed flood requests. Its **first appearance (04:16:13.599) is ~1 min 13 s after onset (04:15)** — the Anti-DDoS detection engaged essentially immediately as volume spiked.
- `awswaf:managed:token:absent` is present throughout (baseline + flood) and reflects requests arriving without a WAF token.
- **No** `...anti-ddos:ddos-event-detected`-style label, and **no** `awswaf:managed:captcha:*` labels were observed. These requests were marked "challengeable" but the rate-based rule took the terminating BLOCK action rather than issuing a challenge.

## 5. Attacker characteristics (flood window 04:15–04:22, BLOCK)
Distributed botnet of **10 source IPs**, each contributing a near-identical ~55,000–58,000 requests (highly even = coordinated/scripted):

| clientIp | Country | BLOCKed reqs |
|---|---|---|
| 47.129.153.245 | SG | 57,691 |
| 54.179.169.215 | SG | 57,600 |
| 65.2.111.194 | IN | 57,078 |
| 54.171.225.201 | IE | 57,013 |
| 108.130.203.106 | IE | 57,010 |
| 18.237.194.213 | US | 56,950 |
| 44.192.247.201 | US | 56,642 |
| 3.238.251.86 | US | 55,699 |
| 44.244.75.242 | US | 55,458 |
| 13.207.5.101 | IN | 54,929 |

- **Countries:** US, SG, IN, IE (geographically distributed).
- **User-Agent (100% of flood):** `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/125.0.0.0 Safari/537.36`
- **JA3 fingerprint (100% of flood):** `473cd7cb9faa642487833865d516e578` — single uniform TLS fingerprint, a strong automated-bot signature.
- **Target URI (100%):** `/`
- **Baseline contrast (02:00–02:30):** 951 requests, 100% ALLOW, a *different* single JA3 `06b2d3d070485ee2907911c00c8b2803`, from many `15.177.x.x` IPs (~60 req each — AWS/CloudFront monitoring range). The flood JA3, UA uniformity, and 10-IP structure are entirely distinct from legitimate baseline traffic.

## 6. Recovery
- **ALLOW stopped leaking to the flood** after 04:16: from 04:17 onward ALLOW returns to baseline (~31–32/min) while BLOCK carries the full ~120K/min — WAF was effectively blocking the attack within ~1 minute of onset.
- **Raw flood volume dropped** at 04:21 (16,092) and fully returned to baseline (~31/min) by **04:22** — attacker ceased.
- Net: WAF mitigation (rate-limit + anti-ddos labeling) was effective; only a ~31,662-request burst leaked during the initial 04:16 ramp before the rate threshold engaged.

**Summary:** A ~7-minute distributed HTTP flood (onset 04:15, peak ~120K req/min 04:17–04:19, over by 04:22) from a 10-IP botnet with a single JA3 (`473cd7cb9faa642487833865d516e578`) and uniform Chrome UA hitting `/`. AWS WAF's **rate-based rule `rate-limit`** BLOCKed **566,070** requests, with the AWS Anti-DDoS managed rule group stamping **`awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`** on every blocked request starting **04:16:13 UTC**. No challenge/captcha was issued; mitigation was pure BLOCK and fully effective after a brief ~31K-request leak during the 04:16 ramp.

# WAFv2 Analysis — DDoS Flood on cf-httpecho.a.example.com (shield-sample-webacl)

**Account 012345678901_1 · us-east-1 · namespace AWS/WAFV2 · Period=300 (5-min) · window 2026-09-08 00:00–06:30 UTC**

## Headline Findings

- The flood was a single, sharp **~10-minute spike centered at 04:15 UTC**. It was **blocked almost entirely by the custom `rate-limit` rule (priority 6)** — that rule accounts for **100%** of the WebACL's blocked volume.
- The **Anti-DDoS managed rule group did detect the event** — it labeled every flood request `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` — but it took **no server-side block/challenge action** itself. All its action-level counters (DDoSRequests, ChallengeDDoSRequests, ChallengeAllDuringEvent, ManagedRuleGroup-level Blocked/Challenge/Counted) are **empty/zero**. The actual blocking was done downstream by `rate-limit`.
- **No client-side challenges were issued** (ChallengeRequests, ChallengesAttempted, ChallengesSolved, RequestsWithValidChallengeToken, SampleChallengeRequest are all empty for the window) — consistent with the flood being blocked outright by the rate limiter before any challenge flow mattered.

## Timeline (5-minute buckets, UTC)

| Time (UTC) | Allowed (ALL) | Blocked (ALL) | Counted (ALL) | rate-limit Blocked | anti-ddos label `challengeable-request` Blocked | Phase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 00:00 – 04:10 | ~157–160 each bucket (flat) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **Baseline** |
| **04:15** | **34,088** | **432,530** | **33,930** | **432,530** | **432,530** | **Flood onset / peak** |
| **04:20** | 159 | **133,540** | 0 | **133,540** | **133,540** | **Tail / decay** |
| 04:25 – 06:25 | ~156–160 each bucket (flat) | 0 | 0 (one stray `2` at 05:25) | 0 | 0 | **Recovery (baseline)** |

### Quantified
- **Onset:** 04:15:00Z (nothing elevated in the 04:10 bucket; the 04:10 Allowed value was a normal 160).
- **Peak:** 04:15:00Z bucket.
- **Peak blocked volume:** **432,530 requests / 5 min** (plus 133,540 in the following bucket → **566,070 total blocked** across the two buckets).
- **Peak allowed volume:** 34,088 req/5min vs **~159 req/5min baseline → ~214× the normal allowed rate.**
- **Total flood magnitude at 04:15:** 34,088 allowed + 432,530 blocked ≈ **466,618 requests in that single 5-min bucket** (~1,555 req/sec).
- **Return to baseline:** by **04:25:00Z** (Allowed back to ~159, Blocked back to 0). Total disruption window ≈ 10 minutes (04:15–04:25).

## What stopped the flood — per-rule attribution
- **`rate-limit` (priority 6, RateBasedStatement, Block, Limit 100 / 300s / IP):** 432,530 blocked @04:15, 133,540 @04:20. **This is the sole blocking rule** — its values match the WebACL-level BlockedRequests exactly, bucket for bucket. This is the rule that stopped the flood.
- **IP reputation (`AWS-AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList`, priority 5):** 0 blocks (empty at both Rule and ManagedRuleGroup dimension) — did not engage.
- **CommonRuleSet / KnownBadInputs / BotControl / SQLi:** 0 blocks during the window — the flood was volumetric, not signature/content-based.
- **CountedRequests = 33,930 @04:15:** attributable to the Count-action rules at the top of the ACL (allow-internal-monitoring / allow-search-engines were queried and returned empty, so the count came from the managed rule groups running in Count/override and the Anti-DDoS captcha-absent label match, which tracks baseline+34,088). This is observe-only and did not block anything.

## Anti-DDoS rule group behavior (priority 4, OverrideAction None, client-side Challenge HIGH, SensitivityToBlock LOW)
- **Detection: YES.** The label `LabelName=challengeable-request, LabelNamespace=awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos` shows **BlockedRequests = 432,530 @04:15 and 133,540 @04:20** — i.e., every blocked flood request carried the anti-ddos `challengeable-request` label. The rule group first engaged in the **same 04:15 bucket as onset** (no earlier engagement visible at 5-min resolution).
- The same anti-ddos label on **AllowedRequests** tracks the full traffic shape (baseline 159 + the 34,088 at 04:15), confirming the rule group evaluated and labeled all traffic, legitimate and flood alike.
- **Action by the rule group itself: NONE.** Every ManagedRuleGroup-dimension Anti-DDoS metric — Blocked/Challenge/Counted at group level and the per-rule DDoSRequests / ChallengeDDoSRequests / ChallengeAllDuringEvent — returned **empty**. The `awswaf:managed:token` and `awswaf:managed:captcha` block/counted context metrics also returned empty (only the broad captcha-`absent` CountRuleMatch tracked baseline+34,088). So the Anti-DDoS group operated as a **labeler/detector only**; the block decision was executed by the downstream `rate-limit` rule matching those labeled requests.

### Exact anti-ddos label strings observed with counts
- `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` — BlockedRequests: 432,530 (04:15), 133,540 (04:20); AllowedRequests: ~159/bucket baseline + 34,088 (04:15).

## Data notes / caveats
- Per retention rules, 1-minute data (>15 days old) is expired; all values are **5-minute (Period=300)** sums, which is why onset/peak collapse into the single 04:15 bucket. Finer sub-5-min timing (e.g., exact second of onset) is not recoverable from CloudWatch.
- CloudFront-scope WebACL metrics carry **no Region dimension** — queries used `WebACL=shield-sample-webacl` (+ `Rule=ALL` for WebACL-level). All queries succeeded against account 012345678901_1 / us-east-1.
- There is **no `Rule=AWS-AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet` dimension**; the Anti-DDoS group reports via `ManagedRuleGroup=AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet`, `Context=AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet`, and `LabelNamespace=awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos` dimensions (all enumerated above).

**Bottom line:** A ~1,555 req/s volumetric flood hit at 04:15 UTC and lasted ~10 minutes. The Anti-DDoS managed rule group detected it (labeling 566K requests `challengeable-request`) but did not itself block or challenge; the custom **`rate-limit` rule absorbed and blocked the entire flood** (432,530 then 133,540 requests), and traffic returned to the ~159 req/5min baseline by 04:25 UTC.

## 1. LABEL SEMANTICS

### `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` — what it actually means

This label is **NOT a DDoS-detection signal**. It is a per-request *capability* flag that says "this request's URI could take a silent browser challenge." Quoting the Dev Guide:

> "`awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` – Indicates that the request URI is capable of handling the Challenge action. The managed rule group applies this to **any request whose URI isn't exempted**. URIs are exempted if they match the rule group's exempt URI regular expressions."
> "Only `GET` requests are challengeable; the rule group never applies this label to requests that use other methods."

The API Reference for `ClientSideAction.UsageOfAction` confirms it is applied broadly (not only during an attack):

> "If usage is enabled: The managed rule group adds the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` to **any web request that does not match the regular expressions provided in** `ExemptUriRegularExpressions`."

**Direct answers to your sub-questions:**
- **Applied to every request, or only during a detected DDoS event?** → It is applied to essentially **every (eligible: `GET`, non-exempt URI) request the rule group inspects** when `UsageOfAction=ENABLED`, regardless of whether a DDoS event is in progress. It is a URI-eligibility label, not an attack-state label.
- **Does its presence by itself mean a DDoS event was detected/declared?** → **No.** The event-detection label is a *different* label (`event-detected`, below). `challengeable-request` carries no detection meaning. (The two rules that *act* on `challengeable-request` only do so during an event — but the *label itself* is added independent of event state.)

### `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`
> "Matches requests that have the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` **for any protected resource that is currently under attack**. **Rule action: Challenge.** You can only override this rule action to Allow or Count. ### `ChallengeDDoSRequests`

## 3. CLIENT-SIDE ACTION + `SensitivityToBlock`

These are **two independent sensitivity knobs** controlling **two independent mitigation types**:

### `ClientSideActionConfig.Challenge` (the soft/challenge path)
- `UsageOfAction=ENABLED` → the group (a) adds `challengeable-request` to all eligible requests, and (b) **enables and evaluates `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` and `ChallengeDDoSRequests`** during an event:
  > "The two rules are evaluated against web requests for protected resources that are experiencing a DDoS attack. The two rules only apply their action to matching requests that have the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`."
- `Sensitivity` (the Challenge sensitivity, default `HIGH` per the `ClientSideAction` API) controls **how aggressively `ChallengeDDoSRequests` challenges**:
  > "Low… match only on the … high suspicion label … Medium … medium and high … High … all of the suspicion labels: low, medium, and high."
  With `Sensitivity=HIGH`, `ChallengeDDoSRequests` would match requests at **all** suspicion levels (low/medium/high) — i.e., challenge very broadly. *(Note: `ChallengeDDoSRequests` only runs at all if `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` is overridden to Count; otherwise `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` challenges everything challengeable and `Sensitivity` is moot.)*

### `SensitivityToBlock` (the hard/block path, used by `DDoSRequests`)
- Default `LOW`. From the API Reference:
  > "**Low sensitivity is less sensitive, causing the rule to match only on the most likely participants in an attack, which are the requests with the high suspicion label** `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:high-suspicion-ddos-request`. Medium … medium and high … High … all … low, medium, and high."

### Putting your scenario together (Challenge `UsageOfAction=ENABLED, Sensitivity=HIGH` + `SensitivityToBlock=LOW`), during a detected event:
- **Blocked:** `DDoSRequests` blocks only requests carrying `high-suspicion-ddos-request` (because `SensitivityToBlock=LOW` = least aggressive blocking → **only the highest-confidence attack participants are blocked**).
- **Silently Challenged:** the challenge rules challenge `challengeable-request` requests. With default `ChallengeAllDuringEvent=Challenge`, **all challengeable (GET, non-exempt) requests get the silent challenge**; `Sensitivity=HIGH` only becomes relevant if you flip `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` to Count, in which case `ChallengeDDoSRequests` challenges all suspicion levels (low+medium+high).
- **Net effect of `SensitivityToBlock=LOW`:** it narrows hard blocking to the smallest, highest-confidence set (high-suspicion only), leaving medium/low-suspicion requests to be handled by the softer challenge path (or passed through if not challengeable). It is the **least aggressive** blocking setting.

## 4. DETECTION MECHANISM & TERMINATING ACTION

### How "under a DDoS event" is decided
Per the `event-detected` label definition:
> "The managed rule group **detects events when the traffic to the resource has a significant deviation from the resource's traffic baseline**."

So detection is **baseline-deviation-based, performed by the managed rule group itself** on the protected resource's traffic. The documentation for this rule group describes it as self-contained ("Detects, labels, and challenges requests…") and does **not** state that it depends on Shield Advanced's detection to declare the event. (It is part of AWS WAF intelligent-threat-mitigation; the WAF docs don't attribute the detection to Shield.) **I did not find explicit doc text tying event detection to Shield's detector**, so I'd call the "relies on Shield" question **unconfirmed** rather than assert either way.

### Is the challenge a TERMINATING action? Can `challengeable-request` coexist with a different `terminatingRuleId`?

**Yes — a request can carry `anti-ddos:challengeable-request` and have its `terminatingRuleId` be a different, lower-priority rule.** Supporting doc facts:

1. **The label is not an action.** It is added to *all* eligible requests up front (API ref: added to "any web request that does not match … `ExemptUriRegularExpressions`"), completely independent of whether any rule terminates.

2. **The challenge rules only act during an event and only within the group.** If there is **no event**, `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`/`ChallengeDDoSRequests` do not apply their action at all, yet the `challengeable-request` label is still present. Thus the group takes **no terminating action**, and a later lower-priority rule (e.g., your rate-based rule) is free to be the `terminatingRuleId`.

3. **The group "applies labels … but doesn't always act on them."** Dev Guide, verbatim:
   > "The Anti-DDoS managed rule group **applies labels to requests, but doesn't always act on them.** The request management depends on the confidence with which the rule group determines participation in an attack. If you want, you can manage requests that the rule group labels by **adding a label matching rule that runs after the rule group**."
   This explicitly contemplates downstream (lower-priority) rules being the ones that terminate, based on the labels the group added.

4. **Even when the challenge rules do match, overriding `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` to Count** (which the sensitivity-tuning path requires) means the group does **not** terminate on those requests — again leaving a later rule to terminate.

**On whether Challenge is terminating when it *does* fire:** In AWS WAF generally, Challenge is a terminating action for requests lacking a valid token (it returns the interstitial and stops evaluation) but is **non-terminating** for requests with a valid, unexpired token (evaluation continues). So when `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`/`ChallengeDDoSRequests` apply Challenge: a request with a valid token passes the challenge, is **not** terminated by the group, and continues to lower-priority rules that may then terminate it. This mechanism is a second, independent way a `challengeable-request`-labeled request ends up with a different rule as `terminatingRuleId`.

**Bottom line for your log interpretation:** Seeing `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` on a request tells you **only** that the request was a challenge-eligible GET to a non-exempt URI. It does **not** prove a DDoS event was detected (look for `event-detected`), and it does **not** mean the Anti-DDoS group terminated the request — the `terminatingRuleId` can legitimately be a different, lower-priority rule such as a rate-based rule.

Baseline about 31 to 32 req/min, so 2000 per 300s (about 400 req/min) leaves headroom; tune to real peak legitimate volume before applying.\n- Blocking the high-suspicion Anti-DDoS label denies any request the group labels high-suspicion; monitor for false positives after rollout.\n\n**Advisory:**\n- Apply via aws wafv2 update-web-acl with --lock-token FRESH, --default-action Allow, --visibility-config, and --rules file://updated-rules.json (backed-up Rules array plus the three new rules).\n- Consider deploying the new rules in Count mode first to observe match volume, then switch to Block/Challenge once thresholds are confirmed.\n- Keeping the per-IP rate-limit unchanged preserves the defense that stopped this incident; the new rules are strictly additive.","children":[]}]}]}]}]}]}]}}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Traffic flood against cf-httpecho.a.example.com
**Description:** Volumetric HTTP flood against cf-httpecho.a.example.com (CloudFront distribution behind WebACL shield-sample-webacl). Onset 04:15:00 UTC 2026-09-08, peak ~120K req/min / ~1,555 req/s (04:17–04:19), subsided by 04:22, baseline restored by 04:25. ~566,070 requests blocked. Sourced from a 10-IP distributed botnet (SG/IN/IE/US) with uniform JA3/UA hitting URI `/`.
**Time:** 2026-09-08T04:15:00Z - 2026-09-08T04:22:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: rate-limit rule absorbed the flood
**Description:** The WebACL `rate-limit` rule (RATE_BASED, 100 req/300s per IP, Block action at priority 6) blocked the entire flood. Per-rule CloudWatch BlockedRequests for `rate-limit` total 566,070 (432,530 at 04:15 + 133,540 at 04:20), matching the WebACL-total BlockedRequests exactly. The `AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet` managed rule group (priority 4) returned ZERO datapoints for Blocked/Challenge/Counted — it did NOT engage. No Challenge/CAPTCHA actions occurred.
**Cascades to:** symptom-traffic-flood

### Root Cause: External 10-IP botnet HTTP flood
**Description:** The fundamental cause of the symptom: a ~7-minute coordinated distributed HTTP GET flood against `/` on cf-httpecho.a.example.com from a **10-IP botnet** (US/SG/IN/IE), each IP sending ~55K–58K requests, with a single uniform JA3 fingerprint `473cd7cb9faa642487833865d516e578` and uniform Chrome User-Agent. Peak ~1,555 req/s, ~566K+ total requests. This external, input-driven attack is the root driver — no internal code/config change was involved. The attack self-terminated at ~04:22; its deepest source is outside accessible systems.
**Cascades to:** symptom-traffic-flood

### Hypothesis: Single-rule L7-flood defense (defense-in-depth gap)
**Description:** Forward-looking risk (not a cause of this incident): the entire L7-flood mitigation depended solely on the custom per-IP `rate-limit` rule (priority 6; Block; 100 req/300s per IP). A more distributed flood — many source IPs each staying under 100 req/300s — would not trip this per-IP threshold, and the AWS Anti-DDoS managed rule group (priority 4) did not engage as a backstop (it never declared a DDoS event in this incident). There is therefore no secondary L7-flood defense. A WAF-hardening recommendation is being prepared.
**Cascades to:** symptom-traffic-flood

#### Gaps
- **No CloudTrail visibility for account 012345678901_1 / us-east-1:** CloudTrail LookupEvents returned zero events of any kind (mutative AND read-only) across a full month (2026-08-01 → 2026-09-09), despite the incident being only ~39 days ago (within 90-day retention). This is a visibility limitation, not confirmed absence of activity. Consequence: cannot definitively prove via CloudTrail that no human/config change occurred, nor establish when the Anti-DDoS rule group / rate-limit rule were configured. Automated-only mitigation is strongly supported by WAF metrics/logs but not independently corroborated by CloudTrail.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Harden CloudFront WebACL shield-sample-webacl with three additive defense-in-depth rules — an aggregate CONSTANT rate-based Block rule, a label-match Block on the Anti-DDoS high-suspicion label, and a label-match Challenge on medium/low-suspicion labels — without altering any existing rule or the Allow default action. Closes the single-point-of-defense gap (sole reliance on the per-IP rate-limit rule).

## Reasoning
The 2026-09-08 flood was stopped entirely by one per-IP rate-based rule (rate-limit, 100/300s, blocked 566,070 requests); the AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet group never declared an event and took no action. Two gaps remain: (a) a distributed flood where each IP stays under 100/300s would evade the per-IP rule, and (b) ~31,662 requests leaked during the first ramp minute. This is forward-looking hardening — the incident is fully resolved and self-recovered, and no config change caused it (external botnet), so no rollback of a prior change applies.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Capture the current WebACL config as the exact rollback baseline
**Type:** command
```
aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name shield-sample-webacl --scope CLOUDFRONT --id f7e012b0-0915-4efd-84cf-f04428eafb38 --region us-east-1 > baseline.json
```
**Purpose:** Capture the current WebACL config as the exact rollback baseline

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Capture the live LockToken for optimistic locking
**Type:** command
```
aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name shield-sample-webacl --scope CLOUDFRONT --id f7e012b0-0915-4efd-84cf-f04428eafb38 --region us-east-1 --query LockToken --output text
```
**Purpose:** Capture the live LockToken for optimistic locking
**Advisory:** Use this token, not the investigation-time fa7837f3-a6db-41ff-a408-e06d52be5596.

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Add defense-in-depth so protection no longer relies solely on the…
**Type:** text
update-web-acl with the ENTIRE existing Rules array verbatim PLUS three new rules, fresh LockToken, DefaultAction Allow. Order: Anti-DDoS group (4), anti-ddos-label-block, anti-ddos-label-challenge, AmazonIpReputationList, per-IP rate-limit, aggregate-rate-limit, remaining. New rules: (A) anti-ddos-label-block = LabelMatchStatement Scope LABEL Key awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:high-suspicion-ddos-request, Block; (B) anti-ddos-label-challenge = OrStatement of LabelMatch on medium/low-suspicion labels, Challenge; (C) aggregate-rate-limit = RateBasedStatement Limit 2000 EvaluationWindowSec 300 AggregateKeyType CONSTANT, Block.
**Purpose:** Add defense-in-depth so protection no longer relies solely on the per-IP rate-limit; the CONSTANT rule catches distributed floods and label-match rules make Anti-DDoS labels actionable
**Risks:** CONSTANT limit applies to ALL requests; too low blocks legitimate surges. Baseline ~31-32 req/min, 2000/300s leaves headroom; tune to real peak first., Blocking high-suspicion label denies any so-labeled request; monitor false positives.
**Advisory:** Deploy in Count mode first, then switch to Block/Challenge once thresholds confirmed., Leave the per-IP rate-limit unchanged; new rules are strictly additive.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the three new rules are present with correct actions/ordering…
**Type:** command
```
aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name shield-sample-webacl --scope CLOUDFRONT --id f7e012b0-0915-4efd-84cf-f04428eafb38 --region us-east-1 --query WebACL.Rules
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the three new rules are present with correct actions/ordering, originals intact, DefaultAction still Allow

#### 4.2 Confirm the new rules emit CloudWatch metrics
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch list-metrics --namespace AWS/WAFV2 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the new rules emit CloudWatch metrics
**Advisory:** Alarm on aggregate-rate-limit and anti-ddos-label-block BlockedRequests to detect future floods.

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Revert to the pre-change baseline if the new rules cause false…
**Type:** command
```

```
**Purpose:** Revert to the pre-change baseline if the new rules cause false positives; re-fetch a fresh LockToken first
**Risks:** Safety revert of the additive hardening only, NOT a rollback of an incident cause (external botnet).

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the WAFv2 defense-in-depth rules in the WebACL's IaC/CDK definition so the hardening is durable and not lost to drift.
**Description:** Add the three new rules (anti-ddos-label-block Block on the high-suspicion label; anti-ddos-label-challenge Challenge on medium/low-suspicion labels; aggregate-rate-limit CONSTANT rate-based Block at a tuned Limit/300s) to the source-of-truth definition of shield-sample-webacl, with the label-match rules ordered after the Anti-DDoS managed group and the aggregate rate rule alongside the existing per-IP rate-limit. - The existing per-IP rate-limit and all managed rule groups remain unchanged and DefaultAction remains Allow.
- A deploy of the IaC package reproduces the hardened rule set exactly and re-applying reverts any manual drift.

{"id": "69e232d5-ec69-495a-9e85-682532b75bd3", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_GN9ZPRhbYRED2sv3Z7Q3gZ", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-ddos.html\",\"content\":\"Note: Page redirected from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-ddos.html to https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/what-is-aws-waf.html .\\n\\n**Introducing a new console experience for AWS WAF**\\n\\nYou can now use the updated experience to access AWS WAF functionality anywhere in the console.\\nFor more details, see Working with the console.\\n\\n# What are AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, AWS Shield network security director and AWS Firewall Manager?\\n\\nYou can use AWS WAF, AWS Shield, and AWS Firewall Manager together to create a comprehensive\\nsecurity solution. AWS WAF is a web application firewall that you can use to monitor web requests\\nthat your end users send to your applications and to control access to your content.\\nShield Advanced provides protection against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks\\nfor AWS resources, at the network and transport layers (layer 3 and 4) and the application layer (layer 7).\\nAWS Firewall Manager provides management of protections like AWS WAF and Shield Advanced across accounts and resources,\\neven as new resources are added.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* What is AWS WAF?\\n* What is AWS Shield Advanced?\\n* What is AWS Shield network security director?\\n* What is AWS Firewall Manager?\\n\\n## What is AWS WAF?\\n\\nAWS WAF is a web application firewall that lets you monitor the HTTP and HTTPS requests that\\nare forwarded to your protected web application resources. You can protect the following\\nresource types:\\n\\n* Amazon CloudFront distribution\\n* Amazon API Gateway REST API\\n* Application Load Balancer\\n* AWS AppSync GraphQL API\\n* Amazon Cognito user pool\\n* AWS App Runner service\\n* Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway\\n* AWS Verified Access instance\\n* AWS Amplify\\n\\nAWS WAF lets you control access to your content. Based on conditions that you specify,\\nsuch as the IP addresses that requests originate from or the values of query strings, your\\nprotected resource responds to requests either with the requested content, with an HTTP 403\\nstatus code (Forbidden), or with a custom response.\\n\\nAt the simplest level, AWS WAF lets you choose one of the following behaviors:\\n\\n* **Allow all requests except the ones that you\\n  specify** \u2013 This is useful when you want Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, AWS AppSync, Amazon Cognito, AWS App Runner, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, or AWS Verified Access to\\n  serve content for a public website, but you also want to block requests from\\n  attackers.\\n* **Block all requests except the ones that you\\n  specify** \u2013 This is useful when you want to serve content for a\\n  restricted website whose users are readily identifiable by properties in web\\n  requests, such as the IP addresses that they use to browse to the website.\\n* **Count requests that match your criteria** \u2013 You can\\n  use the Count action to track your web traffic without modifying how you handle it.\\n  You can use this for general monitoring and also to test your new web request\\n  handling rules. When you want to allow or block requests based on new properties in\\n  the web requests, you can first configure AWS WAF to count the requests that match\\n  those properties. This lets you confirm your new configuration settings before you\\n  switch your rules to allow or block matching requests.\\n* **Run CAPTCHA or challenge checks against requests that match your\\n  criteria** \u2013 You can implement CAPTCHA and silent challenge controls\\n  against requests to help reduce bot traffic to your protected resources.\\n\\nUsing AWS WAF has several benefits:\\n\\n* Additional protection against web attacks using criteria that you specify. You\\n  can define criteria using characteristics of web requests such as the\\n  following:\\n\\n  + IP addresses that requests originate from.\\n  + Country that requests originate from.\\n  + Values in request headers.\\n  + Strings that appear in requests, either specific strings or strings that\\n    match regular expression (regex) patterns.\\n  + Length of requests.\\n  + Presence of SQL code that is likely to be malicious (known as *SQL injection*).\\n  + Presence of a script that is likely to be malicious (known as *cross-site scripting*).\\n* Rules that can allow, block, or count web requests that meet the specified\\n  criteria. Alternatively, rules can block or count web requests that not only meet\\n  the specified criteria, but also exceed a specified number of requests in a minute\\n  or in five minutes.\\n* Rules that you can reuse for multiple web applications.\\n* Managed rule groups from AWS and AWS Marketplace sellers.\\n* Real-time metrics and sampled web requests.\\n* Automated administration using the AWS WAF API.\\n\\nIf you want granular control over the protections that you add to your resources, AWS WAF\\nalone might be the right choice. For more information about AWS WAF, see AWS WAF.\\n\\n## What is AWS Shield Advanced?\\n\\nYou can use AWS WAF web access control lists (web ACLs) to help minimize the effects of a\\nDistributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack. For additional protection against DDoS\\nattacks, AWS also provides AWS Shield Standard and AWS Shield Advanced. AWS Shield Standard is\\nautomatically included at no extra cost beyond what you already pay for AWS WAF and your\\nother AWS services.\\n\\nShield Advanced provides expanded DDoS attack protection for your\\nAmazon EC2 instances, Elastic Load Balancing load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Route 53 hosted zones, and AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerators.\\nShield Advanced incurs additional charges. Shield Advanced options and features include automatic application layer DDoS mitigation, advanced event visibility, and dedicated\\nsupport from the Shield Response Team (SRT). If you own high visibility websites or are otherwise\\nprone to frequent DDoS attacks, consider purchasing the additional protections that\\nShield Advanced provides. For additional information, see AWS Shield Advanced capabilities and options and Deciding whether to subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced and apply additional protections.\\n\\n## What is AWS Shield network security director?\\n\\nAWS Shield network security director helps secure your AWS environment by discovering your compute, networking, and network security resources across your account.\\nnetwork security director evaluates each resource's security configuration by analyzing network topology and security configurations against AWS best practices and threat intelligence.\\nTo help you strengthen your security, network security director rates its findings from low to critical severity and shares specific remediation steps, which you can explore using natural language queries through Amazon Q Developer.\\n\\nFor more information about AWS Shield network security director, see AWS Shield network security director (preview).\\n\\n## What is AWS Firewall Manager?\\n\\nAWS Firewall Manager simplifies your administration and maintenance tasks across multiple accounts\\nand resources for a variety of protections, including AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, Amazon VPC security groups and network ACLs,\\nAWS Network Firewall, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall. With Firewall Manager, you set up your protections just once\\nand the service automatically applies them across your accounts and resources, even as you add new accounts and resources.\\n\\nFor more information about Firewall Manager, see AWS Firewall Manager.\",\"total_length\":7150,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":7150,\"truncated\":false,\"redirected_url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/what-is-aws-waf.html\",\"error_code\":null}]}}"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "d09f8803-7df1-441b-98c5-a1cb88e7cebb", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_EWBO2jxzeLLOgC5sDFfM2k", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-ddos-prevention.html\",\"content\":\"Note: Page redirected from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-ddos-prevention.html to https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/what-is-aws-waf.html .\\n\\n**Introducing a new console experience for AWS WAF**\\n\\nYou can now use the updated experience to access AWS WAF functionality anywhere in the console.\\nFor more details, see Working with the console.\\n\\n# What are AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, AWS Shield network security director and AWS Firewall Manager?\\n\\nYou can use AWS WAF, AWS Shield, and AWS Firewall Manager together to create a comprehensive\\nsecurity solution. AWS WAF is a web application firewall that you can use to monitor web requests\\nthat your end users send to your applications and to control access to your content.\\nShield Advanced provides protection against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks\\nfor AWS resources, at the network and transport layers (layer 3 and 4) and the application layer (layer 7).\\nAWS Firewall Manager provides management of protections like AWS WAF and Shield Advanced across accounts and resources,\\neven as new resources are added.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* What is AWS WAF?\\n* What is AWS Shield Advanced?\\n* What is AWS Shield network security director?\\n* What is AWS Firewall Manager?\\n\\n## What is AWS WAF?\\n\\nAWS WAF is a web application firewall that lets you monitor the HTTP and HTTPS requests that\\nare forwarded to your protected web application resources. You can protect the following\\nresource types:\\n\\n* Amazon CloudFront distribution\\n* Amazon API Gateway REST API\\n* Application Load Balancer\\n* AWS AppSync GraphQL API\\n* Amazon Cognito user pool\\n* AWS App Runner service\\n* Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway\\n* AWS Verified Access instance\\n* AWS Amplify\\n\\nAWS WAF lets you control access to your content. Based on conditions that you specify,\\nsuch as the IP addresses that requests originate from or the values of query strings, your\\nprotected resource responds to requests either with the requested content, with an HTTP 403\\nstatus code (Forbidden), or with a custom response.\\n\\nAt the simplest level, AWS WAF lets you choose one of the following behaviors:\\n\\n* **Allow all requests except the ones that you\\n  specify** \u2013 This is useful when you want Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer, AWS AppSync, Amazon Cognito, AWS App Runner, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, or AWS Verified Access to\\n  serve content for a public website, but you also want to block requests from\\n  attackers.\\n* **Block all requests except the ones that you\\n  specify** \u2013 This is useful when you want to serve content for a\\n  restricted website whose users are readily identifiable by properties in web\\n  requests, such as the IP addresses that they use to browse to the website.\\n* **Count requests that match your criteria** \u2013 You can\\n  use the Count action to track your web traffic without modifying how you handle it.\\n  You can use this for general monitoring and also to test your new web request\\n  handling rules. When you want to allow or block requests based on new properties in\\n  the web requests, you can first configure AWS WAF to count the requests that match\\n  those properties. This lets you confirm your new configuration settings before you\\n  switch your rules to allow or block matching requests.\\n* **Run CAPTCHA or challenge checks against requests that match your\\n  criteria** \u2013 You can implement CAPTCHA and silent challenge controls\\n  against requests to help reduce bot traffic to your protected resources.\\n\\nUsing AWS WAF has several benefits:\\n\\n* Additional protection against web attacks using criteria that you specify. You\\n  can define criteria using characteristics of web requests such as the\\n  following:\\n\\n  + IP addresses that requests originate from.\\n  + Country that requests originate from.\\n  + Values in request headers.\\n  + Strings that appear in requests, either specific strings or strings that\\n    match regular expression (regex) patterns.\\n  + Length of requests.\\n  + Presence of SQL code that is likely to be malicious (known as *SQL injection*).\\n  + Presence of a script that is likely to be malicious (known as *cross-site scripting*).\\n* Rules that can allow, block, or count web requests that meet the specified\\n  criteria. Alternatively, rules can block or count web requests that not only meet\\n  the specified criteria, but also exceed a specified number of requests in a minute\\n  or in five minutes.\\n* Rules that you can reuse for multiple web applications.\\n* Managed rule groups from AWS and AWS Marketplace sellers.\\n* Real-time metrics and sampled web requests.\\n* Automated administration using the AWS WAF API.\\n\\nIf you want granular control over the protections that you add to your resources, AWS WAF\\nalone might be the right choice. For more information about AWS WAF, see AWS WAF.\\n\\n## What is AWS Shield Advanced?\\n\\nYou can use AWS WAF web access control lists (web ACLs) to help minimize the effects of a\\nDistributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack. For additional protection against DDoS\\nattacks, AWS also provides AWS Shield Standard and AWS Shield Advanced. AWS Shield Standard is\\nautomatically included at no extra cost beyond what you already pay for AWS WAF and your\\nother AWS services.\\n\\nShield Advanced provides expanded DDoS attack protection for your\\nAmazon EC2 instances, Elastic Load Balancing load balancers, CloudFront distributions, Route 53 hosted zones, and AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerators.\\nShield Advanced incurs additional charges. Shield Advanced options and features include automatic application layer DDoS mitigation, advanced event visibility, and dedicated\\nsupport from the Shield Response Team (SRT). If you own high visibility websites or are otherwise\\nprone to frequent DDoS attacks, consider purchasing the additional protections that\\nShield Advanced provides. For additional information, see AWS Shield Advanced capabilities and options and Deciding whether to subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced and apply additional protections.\\n\\n## What is AWS Shield network security director?\\n\\nAWS Shield network security director helps secure your AWS environment by discovering your compute, networking, and network security resources across your account.\\nnetwork security director evaluates each resource's security configuration by analyzing network topology and security configurations against AWS best practices and threat intelligence.\\nTo help you strengthen your security, network security director rates its findings from low to critical severity and shares specific remediation steps, which you can explore using natural language queries through Amazon Q Developer.\\n\\nFor more information about AWS Shield network security director, see AWS Shield network security director (preview).\\n\\n## What is AWS Firewall Manager?\\n\\nAWS Firewall Manager simplifies your administration and maintenance tasks across multiple accounts\\nand resources for a variety of protections, including AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced, Amazon VPC security groups and network ACLs,\\nAWS Network Firewall, and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall. With Firewall Manager, you set up your protections just once\\nand the service automatically applies them across your accounts and resources, even as you add new accounts and resources.\\n\\nFor more information about Firewall Manager, see AWS Firewall Manager.\",\"total_length\":7150,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":7150,\"truncated\":false,\"redirected_url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/what-is-aws-waf.html\",\"error_code\":null}]}}"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "b5cfa1b6-b053-4279-a512-15ed62c978f6", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_5DQWfFyty9vBgOraoNuzl6", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/APIReference/API_ClientSideAction.html\",\"content\":\"# ClientSideAction\\n\\nThis is part of the `AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet`\\n`ClientSideActionConfig` configuration in `ManagedRuleGroupConfig`.\\n\\n## Contents\\n\\n**UsageOfAction**\\n:   Determines whether to use the `AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet` rules `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` and `ChallengeDDoSRequests` in the rule group evaluation and the related label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`.\\n\\n    * If usage is enabled:\\n\\n      + The managed rule group adds the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` to any web request that does not match the regular expressions provided in the\\n        `ClientSideAction` setting `ExemptUriRegularExpressions`.\\n      + The two rules are evaluated against web requests for protected resources that are experiencing a DDoS attack.\\n        The two rules only apply their action to matching requests that have the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`.\\n    * If usage is disabled:\\n\\n      + The managed rule group doesn't add the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` to any web requests.\\n      + The two rules are not evaluated.\\n      + None of the other `ClientSideAction` settings have any effect.\\n\\n    **Note:**\\n\\n    This setting only enables or disables the use of the two anti-DDOS rules `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` and `ChallengeDDoSRequests` in the anti-DDoS managed rule group.\\n\\n    This setting doesn't alter the action setting in the two rules. To override the actions\\n    used by the rules `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` and `ChallengeDDoSRequests`,\\n    enable this setting, and then override the rule actions in the usual way, in your managed rule group configuration.\\n\\n    Type: String\\n\\n    Valid Values: `ENABLED | DISABLED`\\n\\n    Required: Yes\\n\\n**ExemptUriRegularExpressions**\\n:   The regular expression to match against the request's host followed by its normalized URI path, used to identify requests\\n    that can't handle a silent browser challenge. When the `ClientSideAction` setting `UsageOfAction` is enabled,\\n    the managed rule group uses this setting to determine which requests to label with\\n    `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`. If `UsageOfAction` is disabled, this setting\\n    has no effect and the managed rule group doesn't add the label to any requests.\\n\\n    AWS WAF matches against the host immediately followed by the normalized URI path and doesn't include the scheme,\\n    the query string, or the fragment. For example, `www.example.com/api/orders`. Because the match begins with the host,\\n    a pattern anchored to the start of the path, such as `^/api/`, never matches. AWS WAF normalizes the path first,\\n    removing empty segments (including a trailing slash) and single-dot (`.`) segments and resolving double-dot (`..`) segments,\\n    so `/api/` is evaluated as `/api`. Only `GET` requests are challengeable.\\n\\n    The anti-DDoS managed rule group doesn't\\n    evaluate the rules `ChallengeDDoSRequests` or `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` for web requests that match this regex. This\\n    is true regardless of whether you override the rule action for either of the rules in your web ACL configuration.\\n\\n    AWS recommends using a regular expression.\\n\\n    This setting is required if `UsageOfAction` is set to `ENABLED`. If required, you can provide\\n    between 1 and 5 regex objects in the array of settings.\\n\\n    AWS recommends starting with the following setting. Review and update it for your application's needs:\\n\\n    `\\\\/api(\\\\/|$)|\\\\.(acc|avi|css|gif|jpe?g|js|mp[34]|ogg|otf|pdf|png|tiff?|ttf|webm|webp|woff2?)$`\\n\\n    Type: Array of Regex objects\\n\\n    Required: No\\n\\n**Sensitivity**\\n:   The sensitivity that the rule group rule `ChallengeDDoSRequests` uses when matching against the\\n    DDoS suspicion labeling on a request. ## 1. LABEL SEMANTICS

### `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` — what it actually means

This label is **NOT a DDoS-detection signal**. It is a per-request *capability* flag that says "this request's URI could take a silent browser challenge." Quoting the Dev Guide:

> "`awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` – Indicates that the request URI is capable of handling the Challenge action. The managed rule group applies this to **any request whose URI isn't exempted**. URIs are exempted if they match the rule group's exempt URI regular expressions."
> "Only `GET` requests are challengeable; the rule group never applies this label to requests that use other methods."

The API Reference for `ClientSideAction.UsageOfAction` confirms it is applied broadly (not only during an attack):

> "If usage is enabled: The managed rule group adds the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` to **any web request that does not match the regular expressions provided in** `ExemptUriRegularExpressions`."

**Direct answers to your sub-questions:**
- **Applied to every request, or only during a detected DDoS event?** → It is applied to essentially **every (eligible: `GET`, non-exempt URI) request the rule group inspects** when `UsageOfAction=ENABLED`, regardless of whether a DDoS event is in progress. It is a URI-eligibility label, not an attack-state label.
- **Does its presence by itself mean a DDoS event was detected/declared?** → **No.** The event-detection label is a *different* label (`event-detected`, below). `challengeable-request` carries no detection meaning. (The two rules that *act* on `challengeable-request` only do so during an event — but the *label itself* is added independent of event state.)

## 2. RULES IN THE GROUP

Rule group identity: `VendorName: AWS, Name: AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet, WCU: 50`.

The group offers **"soft mitigation"** (silent browser challenge) and **"hard mitigation"** (block), both independently tunable by suspicion level. Three rules are documented:

### `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`
> "Matches requests that have the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` **for any protected resource that is currently under attack**. **Rule action: Challenge.** You can only override this rule action to Allow or Count. The use of Allow is not recommended. For any rule action setting, the rule only matches requests that have the `challengeable-request` label. The configuration of this rule affects the evaluation of the next rule, `ChallengeDDoSRequests`. AWS WAF only evaluates that rule when the action for this rule has override set to Count."
> Labels: `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:ChallengeAllDuringEvent`

- **Default action: Challenge.** Acts **only during a detected event**, and only on `challengeable-request`-labeled requests. By default it challenges **all** challengeable requests during the event.

### `ChallengeDDoSRequests`
> "Matches requests for a protected resource that meet or exceed the rule group's configured challenge sensitivity setting, **during times that the resource is under attack. Rule action: Challenge.** You can only override this rule action to Allow or Count… the rule only matches requests that have the `challengeable-request` label. AWS WAF **only evaluates this rule if you override the action to Count in the prior rule, `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`**."
> Labels: `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:ChallengeDDoSRequests`

- **Default action: Challenge.** Acts only during an event, only on `challengeable-request`-labeled requests, and only matches those meeting the `ClientSideAction.Sensitivity` threshold. **It is gated**: it runs only if `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` is overridden to Count.

> "The sensitivity that the rule group rule `DDoSRequests` uses when matching against the DDoS suspicion labeling on a request. The managed rule group adds the labeling during DDoS events, **before the `DDoSRequests` rule runs**."

## 3. CLIENT-SIDE ACTION + `SensitivityToBlock`

These are **two independent sensitivity knobs** controlling **two independent mitigation types**:

### `ClientSideActionConfig.Challenge` (the soft/challenge path)
- `UsageOfAction=ENABLED` → the group (a) adds `challengeable-request` to all eligible requests, and (b) **enables and evaluates `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` and `ChallengeDDoSRequests`** during an event:
  > "The two rules are evaluated against web requests for protected resources that are experiencing a DDoS attack. The two rules only apply their action to matching requests that have the label `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request`."
- `Sensitivity` (the Challenge sensitivity, default `HIGH` per the `ClientSideAction` API) controls **how aggressively `ChallengeDDoSRequests` challenges**:
  > "Low… match only on the … high suspicion label … Medium … medium and high … High … all of the suspicion labels: low, medium, and high."
  With `Sensitivity=HIGH`, `ChallengeDDoSRequests` would match requests at **all** suspicion levels (low/medium/high) — i.e., challenge very broadly. *(Note: `ChallengeDDoSRequests` only runs at all if `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` is overridden to Count; otherwise `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` challenges everything challengeable and `Sensitivity` is moot.)*

### `SensitivityToBlock` (the hard/block path, used by `DDoSRequests`)
- Default `LOW`. From the API Reference:
  > "**Low sensitivity is less sensitive, causing the rule to match only on the most likely participants in an attack, which are the requests with the high suspicion label** `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:high-suspicion-ddos-request`. Medium … medium and high … High … all … low, medium, and high."

### Putting your scenario together (Challenge `UsageOfAction=ENABLED, Sensitivity=HIGH` + `SensitivityToBlock=LOW`), during a detected event:
- **Blocked:** `DDoSRequests` blocks only requests carrying `high-suspicion-ddos-request` (because `SensitivityToBlock=LOW` = least aggressive blocking → **only the highest-confidence attack participants are blocked**).
- **Silently Challenged:** the challenge rules challenge `challengeable-request` requests. With default `ChallengeAllDuringEvent=Challenge`, **all challengeable (GET, non-exempt) requests get the silent challenge**; `Sensitivity=HIGH` only becomes relevant if you flip `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` to Count, in which case `ChallengeDDoSRequests` challenges all suspicion levels (low+medium+high).
- **Net effect of `SensitivityToBlock=LOW`:** it narrows hard blocking to the smallest, highest-confidence set (high-suspicion only), leaving medium/low-suspicion requests to be handled by the softer challenge path (or passed through if not challengeable). It is the **least aggressive** blocking setting.

## 4. DETECTION MECHANISM & TERMINATING ACTION

### How "under a DDoS event" is decided
Per the `event-detected` label definition:
> "The managed rule group **detects events when the traffic to the resource has a significant deviation from the resource's traffic baseline**."

So detection is **baseline-deviation-based, performed by the managed rule group itself** on the protected resource's traffic. The documentation for this rule group describes it as self-contained ("Detects, labels, and challenges requests…") and does **not** state that it depends on Shield Advanced's detection to declare the event. (It is part of AWS WAF intelligent-threat-mitigation; the WAF docs don't attribute the detection to Shield.) **I did not find explicit doc text tying event detection to Shield's detector**, so I'd call the "relies on Shield" question **unconfirmed** rather than assert either way.

### Is the challenge a TERMINATING action? Can `challengeable-request` coexist with a different `terminatingRuleId`?

**Yes — a request can carry `anti-ddos:challengeable-request` and have its `terminatingRuleId` be a different, lower-priority rule.** Supporting doc facts:

1. **The label is not an action.** It is added to *all* eligible requests up front (API ref: added to "any web request that does not match … `ExemptUriRegularExpressions`"), completely independent of whether any rule terminates.

2. **The challenge rules only act during an event and only within the group.** If there is **no event**, `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`/`ChallengeDDoSRequests` do not apply their action at all, yet the `challengeable-request` label is still present. Thus the group takes **no terminating action**, and a later lower-priority rule (e.g., your rate-based rule) is free to be the `terminatingRuleId`.

3. **The group "applies labels … but doesn't always act on them."** Dev Guide, verbatim:
   > "The Anti-DDoS managed rule group **applies labels to requests, but doesn't always act on them.** The request management depends on the confidence with which the rule group determines participation in an attack. If you want, you can manage requests that the rule group labels by **adding a label matching rule that runs after the rule group**."
   This explicitly contemplates downstream (lower-priority) rules being the ones that terminate, based on the labels the group added.

4. **Even when the challenge rules do match, overriding `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` to Count** (which the sensitivity-tuning path requires) means the group does **not** terminate on those requests — again leaving a later rule to terminate.

**On whether Challenge is terminating when it *does* fire:** In AWS WAF generally, Challenge is a terminating action for requests lacking a valid token (it returns the interstitial and stops evaluation) but is **non-terminating** for requests with a valid, unexpired token (evaluation continues). So when `ChallengeAllDuringEvent`/`ChallengeDDoSRequests` apply Challenge: a request with a valid token passes the challenge, is **not** terminated by the group, and continues to lower-priority rules that may then terminate it. This mechanism is a second, independent way a `challengeable-request`-labeled request ends up with a different rule as `terminatingRuleId`.

**Bottom line for your log interpretation:** Seeing `awswaf:managed:aws:anti-ddos:challengeable-request` on a request tells you **only** that the request was a challenge-eligible GET to a non-exempt URI. It does **not** prove a DDoS event was detected (look for `event-detected`), and it does **not** mean the Anti-DDoS group terminated the request — the `terminatingRuleId` can legitimately be a different, lower-priority rule such as a rate-based rule.
